report:
# Can Olive Leaf Extract Reduce High Blood Pressure?

**Yes — the evidence supports this, though it's still an emerging area of research.**

Several controlled human trials point to a genuine antihypertensive effect from olive leaf extract (OLE), largely attributed to its polyphenol content, particularly oleuropein.

**Key evidence:**

The strongest data comes from Susalit et al.'s randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trial comparing OLE (500 mg twice daily) directly against captopril, a standard ACE-inhibitor blood pressure medication, in patients with stage-1 hypertension. OLE performed similarly to captopril in lowering both systolic and diastolic blood pressure over the trial period, while also improving lipid profiles ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/)).

A separate randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial testing a phenolic-rich OLE found significant reductions in blood pressure along with favorable changes in vascular and metabolic markers ([link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-016-1188-y](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-016-1188-y)).

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (published in *Diabetology & Metabolic Syndrome*) pooled data from multiple RCTs examining OLE's effects on cardiovascular risk factors, including blood pressure, lipids, and inflammatory markers, reinforcing the consistency of these benefits across studies ([link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-022-00920-y](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-022-00920-y)).

Additionally, a 2026 PLOS ONE randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial specifically examined standardized olive extract's short-term effects on blood pressure in individuals with elevated readings, adding further support in a cardiovascular prevention context ([journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0344278](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0344278)).

**Conclusion:** Multiple RCTs and a meta-analysis consistently show OLE lowers blood pressure, with effects comparable to a standard antihypertensive drug in at least one trial. Evidence quality is good but based on a limited number of studies, so it should complement — not replace — standard hypertension treatment without medical guidance.
